item.passage:
The county spelling bee was held every March in the gym at Harmon Middle School, under the scoreboard, with folding chairs for the parents and a long table for the three judges. Dara Quinn had finished second the year before. This year, everyone said, the winner would be Wen Liang, who was ten, in fifth grade, and read the dictionary the way other children read comic books.

Dara had watched Wen at the regional round in January. On every word, even an easy one, Wen asked the same questions: What is the language of origin? May I have the definition? Is there a root? Dara had decided that the questions were a way of buying time, a trick for nervous spellers, and she had said so to her mother in the car. She studied the way she always had, from a printed list of eleven hundred words, covering each one with an index card and writing it from memory until her hand ached.

By the ninth round, eleven spellers had become two. Dara stepped to the microphone and heard the word "chronometer."

It had been on no list she had seen. She could hear the pieces of it, but she could hear several ways to put them together, and the clock on the judges' table was running. Then, almost before she had decided to, she asked, "What is the language of origin?"

"Greek," said the pronouncer.

"Is there a root that means time?"

The pronouncer glanced at the judges. "The word comes from the Greek chronos, meaning time, and metron, meaning measure."

Chronos. She had spelled chronic and chronicle a hundred times at the kitchen table. Dara spelled the word slowly, letter by letter, and the bell stayed silent.

Wen came next and missed "bouillon" by a single vowel. Under the rules, Dara had to spell that word and then one more. She spelled "bouillon," which she had once copied out twenty times, and then "trellis," which she had known since she was eight, and the bee was over.

Afterward, while parents folded chairs, Wen walked over to her and said, "You asked for the origin."

"I did," said Dara.

"It works on almost everything," Wen said, and went to find a ride home.

In the car Dara took out her printed list. Beside the first word, in small letters, she wrote where it came from. Then she did the same beside the second.

The pole turns before the door unlocks,
red climbing over white and getting nowhere,
and by eight the three chairs along the window
are taken by men who have brought their own newspapers.

Mr. Ferrante does not hurry. He shakes the cape
out once, like a flag, and settles it on a shoulder
the way you would cover a birdcage at night,
and then he asks the question he asks everyone:

the usual? Most say yes. A few explain at length,
holding a hand above an ear to show the height
they want, and he listens to the whole of it
with his comb held still, then cuts it his own way.

The radio is on low, a ball game from somewhere
it is already afternoon. Somebody has an opinion
about the pitcher. Somebody else has a better one.
The talk goes around the room like a dish of mints

and comes back to the chair, where Mr. Ferrante
says only Is that right, is that right,
and turns the head beneath his hand
a quarter inch toward the light.

My brother is next. He is six and climbs
onto the board laid across the arms of the chair
so that the mirror can find him. He watches
the scissors in the glass as if they were someone else's.

The barber works around the ear the slowest,
his breath held, as if a boy's ear were the one
thing in the shop that could be broken.
When he is done he holds up the hand mirror

so my brother can see the back of his own head,
which none of us ever sees, and my brother nods
the way the men nod, and is lifted down.
By noon the broom has gone across the floor

and gathered everything into one soft heap,
the gray, the black, the sandy, the six-year-old's,
the whole town's Saturday in the dustpan,
and the pole outside still climbing, still getting there.

My grandmother's typewriter came to our house in a black case the size of a small suitcase, the summer she moved into the apartment over my aunt's garage and could keep only what would fit in two rooms. It was a Royal portable, older than my mother. My grandmother had typed on it every Sunday for forty years: letters to her sister in Oregon, to her cousins, to me at camp. Somewhere between the old house and ours, the carriage had jammed and half the keys had stuck.

I was fifteen and had never taken apart anything more complicated than a flashlight. I found a repair manual from 1952 at the library and spread a bedsheet over the dining room table so that every screw would stay where I set it. For three weeks I spent my evenings with a set of jeweler's screwdrivers, a can of mineral spirits, and an old toothbrush, scrubbing forty years of dust and dried oil out of the machine. When a key stuck, I traced its linkage back, piece by piece, until I found the spring that had slipped.

The last problem was the letter t. On my test pages it printed a little above the line, so that every word containing it seemed to hop. The manual explained how to correct this, and I did it, bending the arm of the type bar a hair at a time with a pair of pliers until the t sat level with its neighbors.

The day I brought the typewriter to her apartment, I rolled in a sheet and asked her to try it. She typed her name, then the date, then a whole line about the weather. Then she stopped and looked at the page for a long time.

"You fixed the t," she said.

I said I had, and I explained about the type bar and the pliers. She nodded and told me it was beautiful work. Then she took a shoebox down from her closet shelf and showed me the carbon copies she had kept of her own letters, hundreds of them, and in every one, for forty years, the t hopped above the line. Her sister, she said, used to claim she could tell one of those letters from across the room.

She still types every Sunday. Her letters are clean and even now, and they arrive looking like anyone's. I keep the ones she sent me at camp in a drawer, and sometimes I take one out just to look at the t.

In the winter of 1883 the town of Brennick bought a machine for packing snow. It came by rail in pieces and was assembled in the yard behind the town barn: two wooden drums, each taller than a man and about seven feet wide, set side by side on an iron axle, with a driver's seat perched above them. Six horses pulled it.

The roller was meant to do the opposite of what a modern plow does. In Brennick, as in many northern towns of the time, winter was the easy season for hauling. Farmers brought wood and grain to town on sleighs, and a sleigh moves best over snow that is packed hard and smooth. After every storm the road commissioner, Hiram Clegg, drove the roller along the main road and out the four farm roads, pressing the new snow flat. On a good day the roads were ready for runners by noon.

For nearly thirty years the arrangement suited everyone. Then, in 1911, Dr. Nathan Pryor bought the first automobile in Brennick. Its narrow wheels spun on packed snow, and in deep drifts it stalled entirely. Pryor asked the town to buy a plow and clear the main road down to the gravel, so that he could reach patients in winter.

The farmers objected at the town meeting. A plowed road, they pointed out, was useless to a sleigh; its runners would scrape over bare gravel, and the horses would have to drag a load that had glided easily the day before. One farmer, Ezra Mott, said that the town was being asked to ruin forty miles of good road for the sake of one car.

The meeting reached a compromise. The town bought a plow and kept the roller. Main Street, from the depot to the doctor's house, would be plowed; the farm roads would be rolled. For several winters the two machines went out after each storm in opposite directions, one throwing the snow aside and the other pressing it down.

The compromise lasted only as long as the numbers favored it. By 1920 there were eleven automobiles in Brennick and a motor truck at the creamery, and some of the farmers who had stood with Mott at the meeting had bought trucks of their own. In 1924 the town meeting voted to plow every road. The roller was pushed into the back of the town barn, and its drums were later taken apart for their oak planks, which went into the floor of the new grange hall. Mott, who never owned a truck, drove his sleigh to grange meetings for several more winters, along a plowed road, and tied his horses outside a hall floored with the machine that had once made his road.

item.passage:
Tardigrades are among the smallest animals most people have heard of. Most species are less than a millimeter long, and many are about half that, so to the naked eye one is little more than a speck. Under a microscope a tardigrade looks like a plump, eight-legged bear with claws, lumbering through a drop of water, which is why its common name is water bear. More than a thousand species have been described, living in oceans, lakes and soil and, most famously, in the thin films of water that cling to moss and lichen.

That last home is a strange place for an animal that needs water to move, feed and breathe. A clump of moss on a roof or a wall may be soaked one day and dry as paper the next. Many small animals in such a place would die when the water left. Many tardigrades survive it by drying out along with the moss.

As its surroundings dry, a tardigrade pulls in its head and legs and shrinks into a shape researchers call a tun. It loses nearly all of the water in its body, and its use of energy falls so low that it is hard to measure at all. Some tardigrades have been revived after several years in this state. When water returns, a tun can swell, uncurl and begin walking within minutes to hours.

The tun is remarkably hardy. Dried tardigrades have survived being chilled briefly to temperatures close to absolute zero, and heated far beyond what most animals can bear. In 2007 researchers sent dried tardigrades into orbit on the outside of a spacecraft, and some survived about ten days of exposure to the vacuum of space.

It is tempting, from such reports, to call tardigrades indestructible, but the word is misleading. An active tardigrade, swimming in its drop of water, is a fragile creature that can be killed by conditions far milder than these. Its toughness belongs almost entirely to the dried state and to the process of getting into it slowly; a tardigrade dried too quickly often fails to recover.

How the tun protects itself is still being worked out. Some species fill their cells with a sugar called trehalose, which may help hold delicate molecules in shape as water leaves. Other species make little of that sugar, and researchers have found that many tardigrades produce unusual proteins that seem to form a glassy, protective material as the animal dries. Exactly how these pieces fit together remains one of the open questions about an animal that most people walk past on every mossy wall.

item.passage:
Tardigrades are among the smallest animals most people have heard of. Most species are less than a millimeter long, and many are about half that, so to the naked eye one is little more than a speck. Under a microscope a tardigrade looks like a plump, eight-legged bear with claws, lumbering through a drop of water, which is why its common name is water bear. More than a thousand species have been described, living in oceans, lakes and soil and, most famously, in the thin films of water that cling to moss and lichen.

That last home is a strange place for an animal that needs water to move, feed and breathe. A clump of moss on a roof or a wall may be soaked one day and dry as paper the next. Many small animals in such a place would die when the water left. Many tardigrades survive it by drying out along with the moss.

As its surroundings dry, a tardigrade pulls in its head and legs and shrinks into a shape researchers call a tun. It loses nearly all of the water in its body, and its use of energy falls so low that it is hard to measure at all. Some tardigrades have been revived after several years in this state. When water returns, a tun can swell, uncurl and begin walking within minutes to hours.

The tun is remarkably hardy. Dried tardigrades have survived being chilled briefly to temperatures close to absolute zero, and heated far beyond what most animals can bear. In 2007 researchers sent dried tardigrades into orbit on the outside of a spacecraft, and some survived about ten days of exposure to the vacuum of space.

It is tempting, from such reports, to call tardigrades indestructible, but the word is misleading. An active tardigrade, swimming in its drop of water, is a fragile creature that can be killed by conditions far milder than these. Its toughness belongs almost entirely to the dried state and to the process of getting into it slowly; a tardigrade dried too quickly often fails to recover.

How the tun protects itself is still being worked out. Some species fill their cells with a sugar called trehalose, which may help hold delicate molecules in shape as water leaves. Other species make little of that sugar, and researchers have found that many tardigrades produce unusual proteins that seem to form a glassy, protective material as the animal dries. Exactly how these pieces fit together remains one of the open questions about an animal that most people walk past on every mossy wall.
